"Return all clauses of length at most width meeting these three conditions: 1. Every training window satisfies the clause. 2. Removing any one literal makes it false on at least one training window. 3. At least one window in the declared Cartesian universe falsifies the clause."

✓ Implemented.

"Each rule output is {"clause":[ids],"witnesses":[indices],"counterexample":u}. For each literal in clause order, its witness is the smallest training index where it is the only true literal of this clause. counterexample is the smallest universe index falsifying the entire clause."

✓.

"Sort the rules by (clause length, lexicographic clause IDs)." ✓

"approved is a duplicate-free list of canonical clauses, each length <=width. Some may fail discovery. The effective theory consists exactly of the discovered clauses appearing in approved. Output them as active, ordered like the rules. Do not use unapproved learned clauses during decoding." ✓

Worst case: all 41448 nodes are covering... but then they'd be pruned at level 1 (if a single predicate covers, we prune immediately → few nodes). The worst case for covering-node work: predicates that don't cover alone or in pairs or triples, but all 4-subsets cover. E.g., each predicate true on ~60% of windows: a 3-clause covers w.p. 1-0.4³=0.936 per window; with N=20000 windows, essentially never covers. For all 4-subsets to cover with N large... impossible. With small N (e.g., N=5), many subsets cover → but then pruning kicks in at smaller sizes. The worst case for the number of covering nodes evaluated: N small enough that 4-subsets cover but 3-subsets don't: e.g., each window is falsified by exactly... Let's think: with N=4 windows and 32 predicates each true on exactly 3 of the 4 windows (missing one distinct window), then a clause covers iff its missing-set intersection is empty. 3-subsets: could cover or not. 4-subsets mostly cover. Number of covering nodes ~ C(32,4) = 35960 → each doing minimality (16 ORs of small ints — N=4 bits, so ints are tiny!) → very fast ✓. Since N is small, the big-int ops are trivial. Conversely when N is large (10000 bits), covering nodes are rare. So the cost is self-limiting ✓.

Let me construct that adversarial case anyway and measure: N=4..8 windows, P=32, width=4, U=65536 (so universe ORs of 8KB ints at each covering node: 35960 × 4 ORs × 8KB ≈ 1.1 GB of memory traffic → ~0.5-1s). Hmm, that could be the true worst case. Let me test it.

E.g., let the 4 training windows differ in cells 0..3 (w_k has cell_k = 1, others 0 among cells 0..3 — hmm, need each predicate false on exactly one window).

Simplest: predicate i = `cell_{i mod 4} != (i//4 mod 2)`? Let me think concretely: training windows w0=(0,0,0,0,...), w1=(1,0,0,...), w2=(0,1,0,...), w3=(0,0,1,...) over cells 0..15. Predicate family: for cell c in 0..3: `cell_c == 0` (true on windows where cell_c = 0) and `cell_c == 1`. With 8 predicates per cell (duplicated IDs) → 32 predicates over cells 0..3.

A clause covers all 4 windows iff for each window at least one literal is true. Consider predicates on cell 0: p0 = (c0==0) true on w0,w2,w3; p1 = (c0==1) true on w1. Similarly for cells 1,2,3. A 4-clause covering all windows... e.g., {c0==0, c0==1} covers all 4 windows (2 literals!) → so covering happens at size 2 → pruning at level 2 → few nodes. Not the worst case I wanted.

To force covering only at size 4, I need predicates whose truth sets are such that no ≤3 subset covers but many 4-subsets do. Classic: truth sets = complements of singletons: predicate p_k is false only on window k (true on the other 3). Then a clause covers iff the intersection of their false-sets... a clause covers all 4 windows iff for every window j, some predicate is true on j — since p_k is false only on window k, a clause of predicates {p_a, p_b, ...} fails to cover window j only if ALL its predicates are false on j, i.e., all equal p_j... Since a clause has distinct predicates, at most one predicate is false on any given window → any clause of size ≥2 covers all windows! So size-2 clauses cover → pruning at level 2 → few nodes.

Hmm. To get many covering nodes at level 4, I need: no ≤3-subset covers, but many 4-subsets cover. E.g., N=8 windows; each predicate true on exactly 6 of 8 (false on 2). A 3-clause covers iff the union of their true sets = all 8 iff the intersection of their false sets = ∅. With false-sets of size 2 drawn from 8 windows, three random false-sets intersect... rarely empty? Intersection of 3 random 2-subsets of an 8-set is usually empty → so 3-clauses mostly cover → pruning at level 3. Hmm, need false sets larger: predicate true on 4 of 8 (false on 4). A 3-clause covers iff the 3 false-sets have empty intersection: with random 4-subsets of an 8-set, P(empty intersection) = ? Each element is in a random false-set w.p. 1/2 → P(no element in all 3) = (1-1/8)^8 = 0.34. So ~34% of 3-clauses cover → those prune their subtrees, but 66% continue to level 4 → nodes at level 4 ≈ C(32,4) × 0.66 ≈ 24000 → each covering 4-clause: P(4-clause covers) = (1-1/16)^8 = 0.60 → of the 24000 level-4 nodes, 60% cover → 14000 covering nodes × (minimality check + universe OR). With N=8 (tiny ints) the minimality check is cheap, but the universe OR is on 65536-bit ints (8KB) → 4 ORs per covering node = 32KB → 14000 × 32KB = 450MB of memory traffic ≈ 0.2-0.5s. Plus minimality. So the worst case is maybe ~1s. Fine.

"""Micro-benchmark the discovery worst case directly with synthetic bitsets."""
import random, sys, time
sys.path.insert(0,'/workspace/submission')
from netnomos.learners.exact import discover_clauses

U = 65536
full_u = (1 << U) - 1
rng = random.Random(9)

def rand_mask_universe(density):
    # build a random U-bit int with the given density, fast
    nbytes = (U + 7)//8
    ba = bytearray(rng.randbytes(nbytes))
    return int.from_bytes(ba, 'little') & full_u

def rand_mask_train(n, density):
    nbytes = (n + 7)//8
    bits = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if rng.random() < density:
            bits |= 1 << i
    return bits

for N, dens_t, dens_u in ((8, 0.5, 0.5), (16, 0.5, 0.5), (10000, 0.5, 0.5), (10000, 0.9, 0.9), (4, 0.5, 0.5)):
    P = 32
    tm = [rand_mask_train(N, dens_t) for _ in range(P)]
    um = [rand_mask_universe(dens_u) for _ in range(P)]
    records = list(range(N))
    t = time.time()
    rules = discover_clauses(tm, um, records, U, 4)
    print('N=%-6d dens=%.1f -> %.2fs rules=%d' % (N, dens_t, time.time()-t, len(rules)))
PYEOF
